Name: Reproducibility Project: Psychology
Description: An open, large-scale, collaborative effort to systematically examine the rate and predictors of reproducibility in psychological science, involving 72 researchers from 41 institutions who replicated studies published in three prominent psychological journals in 2008. Main findings: 100 studies attempted; 36 successfully replicated (36% replication rate).
sampling_frame: Rolling pool of 20 articles per journal in publication order from JPSP, Psych Science, JEP:LMC, 2008; teams self-selected on expertise/equipment/population access
schema_source: OSC 2015 Science; per-study outcomes osf.io/fgjvw

Name: Camerer et al. – Experimental Economics Replication Project
Description: A collaborative initiative to replicate influential experimental economics studies published in American Economic Review and the Quarterly Journal of Economics between 2011-2014. Replication statistics: 18 studies attempted; 11 successfully replicated (61.1% replication rate). Key findings: a 61% replication rate with replicated effect sizes being 66% of the original effect sizes.
sampling_frame: Between-subject laboratory experiments published in American Economic Review and Quarterly Journal of Economics, 2011-2014
schema_source: Camerer et al. 2016 Science; VERIFY: confirm all eligible studies attempted

Name: Camerer et al. – Nature/Science Social Science Replication Project
Description: A large-scale replication effort examining the reproducibility of findings across various social science disciplines, including economics, sociology, and political science. Replication statistics: 21 studies attempted; 13 successfully replicated (61.9% replication rate). Key findings: 62% of replications found significant effects in the same direction as originals, though effect sizes averaged about 50% of the original effect sizes, emphasizing the importance of replication in social science research.
sampling_frame: Experimental social science studies published in Nature and Science, 2010-2015; first study reporting a significant treatment effect per paper
schema_source: Camerer et al. 2018 Nat Hum Behav; VERIFY: confirm exhaustiveness

Name: Examining Replicability of Online Experiments (Holzmeister et al.)
Description: Replication of 26 of 41 systematically selected online (MTurk) social-science experiments published in PNAS 2015–2018. The 26 studies were chosen by a decision market in which 162 social scientists traded on replication outcomes: the 12 studies with the highest final market prices, the 12 with the lowest, and 2 selected at random. Replication statistics: 26 experiments attempted; 14 successfully replicated (54% replication rate), with replication effect sizes averaging 45% of the originals. Key finding: the decision market predicted replicability well — 83% of the top-12 group replicated versus 33% of the bottom-12 group.
sampling_frame: 12 highest + 12 lowest prediction-market prices + 2 random draws; conditioned on forecast extremes by construction
schema_source: Holzmeister et al. 2025; aggregate rate is a design artifact - report 83% top vs 33% bottom separately

Name: Many Labs 1
Description: A large collaborative replication project involving 36 labs worldwide that tested 13 classic and contemporary psychological effects across multiple samples and settings. Replication statistics: 13 effects attempted; 10 successfully replicated (≈77% replication rate).Ten effects replicated consistently across sites, while three showed weak or no evidence for the original results. The study demonstrated that many psychological effects are robust across different contexts, though some depend strongly on experimental conditions or sample characteristics.
sampling_frame: Effects chosen for multi-site administrability (short, simple paradigms), not sampled from a frame
schema_source: Klein et al. 2014; NOT the same design as ML3/4/5

Name: Many Labs 2
Description: An extension of Many Labs 1, this project aimed to replicate 28 findings across 125 labs and 36 countries to assess the generalizability of psychological effects. Replication statistics: 28 findings attempted; 14 successfully replicated (50% replication rate). Key findings: The replication rate was approximately 50%, indicating variability in the reproducibility of psychological effects and emphasizing the importance of context, culture, and methodological factors in replication success.
sampling_frame: Effects chosen for multi-site administrability and cross-cultural comparison
schema_source: Klein et al. 2018 AMPPS; ARM UNUSABLE: DB rate 15% vs published ~50% - needs repair

Name: Experimental Philosophy – Reproducibility Project
Description: A collaborative replication project in experimental philosophy (x-phi) that aimed to assess the reproducibility of findings at the intersection of philosophy and psychology. Replication statistics: Approximately 40 experiments attempted; specific replication rates varied by study. Key findings: The project demonstrated variability in replicability across experimental philosophy studies, with some effects replicating consistently while others did not, highlighting the need for rigorous replication in this interdisciplinary field.
sampling_frame: VERIFY: confirm selection procedure in Cova et al. 2018
schema_source: VERIFY: Cova et al. 2018 selection procedure not yet confirmed

Name: Brazilian Reproducibility Initiative
Description: A multicentre initiative in Brazil to assess reproducibility of biomedical experiments run in Brazil (replicated papers needed at least 50% of authors to be based in Brazil). The initiative selected approximately 60 experiments from Brazilian published articles (including cell-viability assays, RT-PCR, and rodent elevated plus maze), with each experiment replicated in 3 laboratories. Replication statistics: 60 experiments attempted; replication success varied between 15% and 45% depending on criteria used. Key findings: Initial results show significant variability in replication success, with replication rates ranging from ~15% to ~45% depending on the specific criteria applied, highlighting challenges in reproducing biomedical research even within the same country's research context.
sampling_frame: Brazilian biomedical experiments sampled on laboratory technique (cell viability/MTT, RT-PCR, elevated plus maze) plus Brazilian authorship - sampled on method, not on findings
schema_source: Brazilian Reproducibility Initiative 2025 bioRxiv

Name: Reproducibility Project: Cancer Biology
Description: The team replicated 50 experiments across 23 high-impact cancer biology papers. They originally set out to replicate 53 papers, but protocol problems, uncooperative authors and others factors forced them to scale back to just 23 papers. The project evaluated 158 reported effects across those papers and found that replication effect sizes were dramatically attenuated, with a median 85% reduction relative to the originals and 92% of replication effect sizes smaller than initially reported. Using five replication criteria applicable to both positive and null findings, only 40% of positive effects and 80% of null effects replicated, yielding an overall replication success rate of 46%. Using a less strict definition of replication (was there a statistically significant effect in the same direction?) the replication rate was 78%.
sampling_frame: High-impact cancer biology papers 2010-2012 selected on citation/impact; 23 of 53 papers survived to completion
schema_source: Errington et al. 2021 eLife; informative censoring - dropout mechanisms proxy the outcome

Name: #EEGManyLabs
Description: An international multi-lab replication project focused on replicating 27 influential electroencephalography (EEG) studies across multiple laboratories. Replication statistics: 27 influential EEG studies attempted; replication rates varied by paradigm and analysis approach. Key findings: Results varied significantly by paradigm and analysis method, demonstrating that EEG findings are context-dependent and highlighting the importance of methodological transparency in neuroscience replication efforts.
sampling_frame: Influential EEG findings chosen by community vote
schema_source: Pavlov et al.; not in DB

Name: Amgen's replication report
Description: Over the course of ten years, scientists in the haematology and oncology department of Amgen tried to confirm published findings in preclinical oncology that were related to their work. In a 2012 commentary in Nature they reported they could only reproduce 6/53 findings (11%). A finding was considered non-reproduced if the finding was "not sufficiently robust to drive a drug-development program".
sampling_frame: Landmark haematology/oncology papers selected internally for drug-programme relevance
schema_source: Begley & Ellis 2012 Nature; criterion is commercial programme viability, not statistical

Name: Bayer Healthcare's replication report
Description: "In a correspondence in Nature Reviews Drug Discovery, three researchers at Bayer Healthcare reported the results of a survey of 23 scientists in their oncology division. They found that across 67 replication attempts, only "~20-25%" yielded results that closely matched the published findings. They reported that 'In almost two-thirds of the projects, there were inconsistencies between published data and in-house data that either considerably prolonged the duration of the target validation process or, in most cases, resulted in termination of the projects because the evidence that was generated for the therapeutic hypothesis was insufficient to justify further investments into these projects.'"
sampling_frame: In-house target-validation projects selected for drug-discovery relevance
schema_source: Prinz et al. 2011 Nat Rev Drug Discov

Name: Boyce et al. – Student Replication Projects
Description: A dataset of 176 replications conducted by graduate students in a methods course over eleven years. Replication statistics: 176 replications attempted; 49% judged successful. Of the 136 replications where effect sizes could be numerically compared, only 46% had point estimates within the prediction interval of the original outcome (versus the expected 95%). Key findings: Larger original effect sizes and within-participants designs were associated with replication success, indicating low robustness in the psychology literature.
sampling_frame: Studies chosen by student replicators on interest and feasibility - the structural twin of MO's literature harvest
schema_source: Boyce et al. 2023 R Soc Open Sci

Name: Motoki and Iseki – Sensory Marketing Replication
Description: A pre-registered replication of ten influential sensory marketing studies conducted online with non-WEIRD (non-Western) consumers in Japan. Replication statistics: 10 studies attempted; 2 successfully replicated (20% replication rate). Key findings: Effect sizes were approximately half of original values. Successful replications involved sound symbolism studies with within-participants designs and larger original sample sizes. No studies involving visual factors, between-participant manipulation, or interactions between factors could be replicated.
sampling_frame: Sensory-marketing effects, conceptual replications in a non-WEIRD (Japanese) sample
schema_source: Motoki & Iseki 2022

Name: Soto – Life Outcomes of Personality Replication Project
Description: A preregistered, high-powered (median N = 1,504) replication of 78 previously published associations between Big Five personality traits and consequential life outcomes. Replication statistics: 78 trait-outcome associations attempted; 68 successfully replicated (87% replication rate). Key findings: 87% of replication attempts were statistically significant in the expected direction. Replication effect sizes were typically 77% as strong as the corresponding original effects, representing a significant but modest decline. Replicability of individual effects was predicted by the effect size and design of the original study, as well as the sample size and statistical power of the replication. These results indicate the personality-outcome literature provides a reasonably accurate map of trait-outcome associations.
sampling_frame: 78 personality-outcome correlations replicated in a single large online sample
schema_source: Soto 2019 Psych Science

Name: Many Labs 5
Description: A follow-up to the Reproducibility Project: Psychology (RP:P) that selected 10 RP:P replication studies for which original authors had expressed concerns about the replication designs. The team revised protocols with formal pre-data-collection peer review and re-ran replications across multiple laboratories (median 6.5 labs per study, median total sample 1,279.5). Key findings: revised protocols produced effect sizes similar to the original RP:P protocols (median r = .05 vs .04). The median effect size across all three replication attempts (r = .07) was 78% smaller than the original effect sizes (median r = .37), with only 1 of 10 studies yielding a statistically significant effect.
sampling_frame: RP:P protocols where original authors objected - conditioned on prior replication failure
schema_source: Ebersole et al. 2020; conditional on prior failure by construction

Name: Estimating the Replicability of Sports and Exercise Science Research
Description: This study aimed to provide an initial estimate of the replicability of applied sports and exercise science research published in quartile 1 journals (SCImago journal ranking for 2019 in the Sports Science subject category) between 2016 and 2021. A formalised selection protocol was previously published. Voluntary collaborators were recruited, and studies were allocated in a stratified and randomised manner on the basis of equipment and expertise. Original authors were contacted to provide deidentified raw data, to review preregistrations and to provide methodological clarifications. In total, 25 replication studies were included for analysis. Of the 25, 10 replications used paired t tests, 1 used an independent t test and 14 used an analysis of variance (ANOVA) for the statistical analyses. In all, 7 (28%) studies demonstrated robust replicability, meeting all three validation criteria: achieving statistical significance (p<0.05) in the same direction as the original study and showing compatible effect size magnitudes as per the Z test (p>0.05). Key findings: There was a substantial decrease in published effect size estimate magnitudes when replicated; therefore, sports and exercise science researchers should consider effect size uncertainty when conducting subsequent power analyses. Additionally, there were many barriers to conducting the replication studies, e.g., original author communication and poor data and reporting transparency.
sampling_frame: Q1 SCImago sports/exercise science journals 2016-2021; stratified/randomised allocation by equipment and expertise
schema_source: Murphy et al. 2025 Sports Med

Name: Social Psychology Special Issue on Registered Replication Reports
Description: A groundbreaking special issue in Social Psychology that pioneered the Registered Reports format for replication studies, edited by Brian A. Nosek and Daniël Lakens. Replication statistics: 14 replication articles published using the registered reports format. The special issue featured replications of classic textbook studies and high-impact contemporary research, including studies on social cognition, moral psychology, embodied cognition, and social exclusion. Key innovations: All studies were preregistered before data collection, with proposals, anonymized data, and study materials registered at the Open Science Framework (OSF). Each article disclosed all conditions, measures, data exclusions, and sample size determinations. The issue demonstrated multiple approaches to impactful replication research: validating classic findings with modern methods, investigating boundary conditions of recent high-impact studies, and resolving contradictory findings in the literature. Results varied across studies, with some classic effects replicating robustly while others showed surprising failures or revealed important moderators. This special issue established a methodological template for transparent, preregistered replication research that has since been adopted widely across psychological science.
sampling_frame: Proposers self-select which effects to submit for registered replication
schema_source: Social Psychology 2014 special issue

Name: Clearer Thinking's Transparent Replication Project
Description: An ongoing rapid replication initiative by Clearer Thinking that conducts independent replications of recently published psychology and human behavior studies from top journals. Unlike other replication projects that focus on older or prominent findings, Transparent Replications randomly selects recent papers from top journals to provide quick feedback on the reliability of new results. Studies are rated on three criteria: Transparency (availability of materials, data, code, and pre-registration adherence; avg 4.1/5), Replicability (proportion of main findings that replicate; avg 4.1/5), and Clarity (likelihood a reader comes away with an accurate impression; avg 3.1/5). Replication statistics (preliminary): 12 replication reports completed; 10 completely or mostly replicated (83% replication rate), substantially higher than the 55% predicted by surveyed psychology experts. Key findings: No clear instances of p-hacking were found in the first 12 replications, suggesting that p-hacking may now be substantially less common than it was 15 years ago. However, the project identified 'Importance Hacking' — obscuring or exaggerating the meaning of results to make them appear more valuable — as a widespread issue affecting most papers, representing what they consider the next major frontier for improving research quality.
sampling_frame: Recent papers from selected high-profile journals; ongoing and preliminary
schema_source: Clearer Thinking Transparent Replications; n=12, subjective 1-5 scoring

Name: Tyner et al. – DARPA SCORE Social & Behavioural Sciences Replication Project
Description: A large-scale, high-powered systematic replication effort conducted as part of the Defense Advanced Research Projects Agency (DARPA) Systematizing Confidence in Open Research and Evidence (SCORE) program. The project replicated 274 quantitative claims drawn from 164 papers published in 54 social and behavioural science journals between 2009 and 2018, spanning six disciplines: business, economics, education, political science, psychology, and sociology. Replications were pre-registered, peer-reviewed, and designed to detect the original effect size with high power (median 99.6%). Replication statistics: 274 claims attempted across 164 papers; 151 claims (55.1%, 95% CI 49.2–60.9%) showed statistically significant results in the same direction as the original finding. At the paper level, 80.8 of 164 papers (49.3%, 95% CI 43.8–54.7%) replicated. Key findings: Replication rates ranged from 42.5% to 63.1% across disciplines. The median Pearson's r effect size was 0.25 in original studies and 0.10 in replications — an 82.4% reduction in shared variance. Thirteen different replication success metrics were applied, yielding success rates ranging from 28.6% to 74.8% (median 49.3%), illustrating the sensitivity of conclusions to the chosen metric.
sampling_frame: Claims drawn from ~3,900 papers across 62 social/behavioural science journals 2009-2018; ~5% went to replication
schema_source: Tyner et al. 2026; VERIFY: confirm draw was random not feasibility-driven (check supplement) - if feasibility-driven downgrade to quasi_random_frame_feasibility

Name: International Initiative for Impact Evaluation Replication Paper Series
Description: A publication and dissemination outlet for internal replication studies of development impact evaluations, run by the International Initiative for Impact Evaluation (3ie) — the global leader in funding, producing, and synthesising high-quality evidence on what works in international development. Internal replications reanalyse data from an original paper to validate its results; the series publishes studies that either reinforce or challenge original findings. To be eligible, a replication must cover a paper in 3ie's Impact Evaluation Repository and must include a pure replication component. 3ie invites formal replies from original authors, published alongside the replication. The programme also funds external replication studies of influential, innovative, or counterintuitive development impact evaluations through periodic grant-making windows. Topics covered include cash transfers, mobile money, land titling, HIV/AIDS interventions, food assistance, and governance reforms in low- and middle-income countries.
sampling_frame: Reanalysis of existing datasets from development impact evaluations; replicators propose targets
schema_source: 3ie Replication Paper Series; reanalysis not new data collection - different construct
exclusion_reason: Reanalysis of the original authors' existing datasets (reproducibility), not new data collection (replicability) - a different construct. DB rows score 13/13 = 100% (2 inconclusive rows excluded from the denominator), which a re-run of the original data largely guarantees. NOTE: its 15 DB rows are also coded replication_type='direct', which is a mislabel for a reanalysis.

Name: Sobkow et al. – Fifteen JDM Effects Conceptual Replication (Polish Sample)
Description: A pre-registered conceptual replication project in which fifteen research teams of undergraduate psychology students at SWPS University (Wroclaw, Poland), coordinated by Agata Sobkow and Jakub Traczyk, replicated 15 classical and modern judgment and decision making (JDM) effects — including anchoring, framing, sunk cost, and less-is-better — adapted to the Polish language, currency, and the COVID-19 pandemic context. All effects were tested in a single online battery completed by 202 Polish Prolific users. Replication statistics: 15 effects attempted; 7 successfully replicated (47% replication rate), 5 partially replicated (33%), and 3 not replicated (20%). Key findings: well-established effects (sunk cost, anchoring, attribute framing, less-is-better) and individual-difference effects largely replicated despite substantial adaptations of materials, while the Tversky & Kahneman (1981) jacket-calculator framing problem and the effort–luxury reward preference effect (Kivetz & Simonson, 2002) failed to replicate, the latter reversing significantly in one scenario. The authors note their replication rate is slightly above earlier comparable projects and stress the role of open data, open materials, and pre-registration in improving replicability in JDM.
sampling_frame: Fifteen JDM effects, conceptual replication with Polish-adapted materials
schema_source: Sobkow et al. 2022
